title: Teaching in an Age of Tech-Created Distraction
author: Justin Reich
source: The Grade, via Alexander Russo (alexanderrusso.substack.com), September 2, 2026
summary: Justin Reich, a former high school history teacher and MIT digital-media professor, argues that the fundamental tradeoff of educational technology, whether accessing a resource is worth navigating its distracting container, has gotten dramatically worse even as the educational software itself has barely improved. Comparing his own 2003 pilot one-to-one laptop classroom to teaching in 2026, he shows the obstacles then were merely clunky (dead batteries, slow WiFi) while today's devices, operating systems, and browsers are deliberately engineered as "heat-seeking missiles for our attention," to the point that he would never assign a student to watch an individual YouTube video today, something unremarkable with RealPlayer in 2003, because neither he nor any student can watch one without being pulled into surrounding distraction. Reich extends the logic that has already produced broad support for school phone bans to take-home devices, screen-based lessons, and AI chatbots specifically, arguing generative AI compounds the underlying problem because "any machine with chatbot to support carefully structured learning is also a machine with a chatbot that will simply give students the answer," making the system less effective for learning even when the pedagogical intent is sound. His conclusion reframes the entire edtech conversation around a single design demand: schools need devices, browsers, and AI tools built to be invisible rather than manipulative, and until that negotiation happens, the pedagogical benefit will not be worth the attentional cost.
points: Reich's twenty-year comparison isolates exactly what changed: the educational software 'has made, at best, modest progress,' while the devices, operating systems, and browsers surrounding it have become dramatically more distracting, meaning the tradeoff worsened not because the tools got worse but because their containers got more manipulative.

His concrete confession, he would never assign an individual YouTube video today though an equivalent RealPlayer assignment was unremarkable in 2003, gives an abstract argument about attention engineering a specific, falsifiable, personal benchmark of how much worse the environment has become.

He extends the logic that already justified school phone bans to the harder cases of take-home devices and AI chatbots explicitly, arguing parents and teachers are 'asking the obvious question: If the phone bans worked so well... why not keep going?' rather than treating bans as a settled, isolated policy.

His critique of AI chatbots in schools is structural, not just behavioral: 'any machine with chatbot to support carefully structured learning is also a machine with a chatbot that will simply give students the answer,' meaning the same tool cannot cleanly separate its supportive and its answer-giving functions.
quotes: And so our devices, browsers, and even now some of our most basic tools have become heat-seeking missiles for our attention.
Then as now, the pedagogical juice has to be worth the technological squeeze.
In 2003, it wasn't crazy to have a student individually follow a link to watch an educational video in RealPlayer. In 2026, I would never direct an individual student to watch a video on YouTube.
For two decades, I believed that edtech's ability to empower and motivate kids was worth the distractions and the junk software. But I'm not so certain anymore.

Any machine with chatbot to support carefully structured learning is also a machine with a chatbot that will simply give students the answer or otherwise do the cognitive work for them. The net effect is to make the entire system less effective for learning.

We need containers that are invisible, not manipulative. And if we can't negotiate ways of wrestling our devices, browsers, search engines, operating systems, and now chatbots into the background of student learning experiences, the juice won't be worth the squeeze.
